column1: What is the key route-specificity invariant distinguishing absorption of water-soluble vs. lipid-soluble macronutrient products?
column2: Water-soluble products (monosaccharides, amino acids) enter capillaries via the hepatic portal vein for first-pass liver metabolism; lipid-soluble products are re-esterified into triglycerides, packaged as chylomicrons, and enter lacteals/lymphatics, bypassing the liver until reaching systemic circulation via the thoracic duct.

column1: What enzymatic cascade processes dietary protein from stomach to brush border?
column2: Pepsin (gastric, acidic lumen) → pancreatic trypsin, chymotrypsin, and elastase (duodenum) → membrane-bound aminopeptidases (brush border), which liberate free amino acids and small dipeptides.

column1: Why must bile salts act before pancreatic lipase can digest triglycerides?
column2: Triglycerides are hydrophobic and would otherwise be inaccessible to water-soluble lipase; bile salts emulsify fat into micelles, presenting triglyceride molecules for lipase to cleave two of three fatty acid ester bonds, yielding monoacylglycerols and free fatty acids.

column1: What is the approximate resting ATP pool size vs. turnover rate during maximal exertion?
column2: ~250 g ATP stored at rest, but turnover can exceed 400 g/min during maximal exertion, requiring continuous multi-pathway regeneration.

column1: Why is the physiological ΔG of ATP hydrolysis (-50 to -60 kJ/mol) different from the standard value (-30.5 kJ/mol)?
column2: Standard ΔG assumes standard conditions, but physiological concentrations of ATP, ADP, and Pi in living cells create a larger free energy gap, meaning cells extract more usable work per hydrolysis event than textbook values suggest.

column1: What are the three ATP regeneration systems and their temporal windows during exercise?
column2: 1) Phosphocreatine (ATP-CP) system: <3 sec onset, saturates ~10 sec. 2) Glycolysis (anaerobic/aerobic): dominates 10 sec–2 min. 3) Oxidative phosphorylation: dominates from 2 min onward, yielding 17-18x more ATP per glucose than anaerobic glycolysis.

column1: What does the phrase 'fats burn in the flame of carbohydrates' mean metabolically?
column2: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids requires adequate oxaloacetate (derived from carbohydrate metabolism) to feed acetyl-CoA into the TCA cycle; without sufficient carbohydrate-derived intermediates, fat oxidation is impaired.

column1: What is the core thermodynamic invariant that prevents futile cycling between opposing metabolic pathways like glycolysis and gluconeogenesis?
column2: Each pathway contains irreversible, committed steps catalyzed by distinct regulatory enzymes (e.g., hexokinase vs. glucose-6-phosphatase) that are reciprocally regulated so opposing pathways aren't simultaneously active, preventing wasteful ATP consumption.

column1: What three enzyme pairs allow gluconeogenesis to bypass the irreversible steps of glycolysis?
column2: 1) Pyruvate carboxylase + PEPCK bypass pyruvate kinase. 2) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses phosphofructokinase-1. 3) Glucose-6-phosphatase bypasses hexokinase.

column1: How does cellular energy charge (ATP:ADP:AMP ratio) act as a metabolic master switch?
column2: High ATP favors anabolic pathways (glycogenesis, lipogenesis); low ATP/high AMP activates AMPK, which phosphorylates and inhibits anabolic enzymes while activating catabolic pathways (glycogenolysis, lipolysis, amino acid oxidation).

column1: What is the first invariant of metabolic regulation regarding flux vs. concentration?
column2: Cells regulate the RATE (flux) of glucose moving through glycolysis to match ATP turnover demand, not merely the presence/concentration of glucose—this is why allosteric, covalent, and hormonal regulation all target reaction velocity.

column1: What is the tissue hierarchy of glucose dependency, and which tissue preferentially uses fatty acids/ketones?
column2: Brain, red blood cells, and renal medulla are obligate glucose consumers. Skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and liver are facultative (substrate-flexible). Cardiac muscle preferentially runs on fatty acids/ketone bodies, reserving glucose for ischemic stress.
